This Gala Apple Tree (Malus domestica) can be found in my backyard. Right now during the summer, is when the apples are growing, so they can be picked and ready to be eaten by fall. When fully ripe and ready to eat, Gala apples have a very sweet taste to them. Delicious for snack or apple pie. description:
I have been observing this crabapple that volunteered along a fence line (almost certainly from bird droppings) for a few years now.  It is not our native crabapple, and doesn't appear to be *M. domestica*, though it could be a hybrid of one of those (or completely unrelated).  It really doesn't seem to match any species description I can find and is almost certainly a hybrid of some sort.  

I have included pictures from bloom time and also fruit both under-ripe, fully ripe and  bletted (a natural softening of the fruit that turns it into edible mush).

The tree is very compact and has quite an upright core with most branches emerging at nearly 90 degree angles.  

If you have any guesses at what the ancestry of this could be I'll be glad to hear your input.

The flavor of the fruit is very citrusy like kumquats, but without the burn.  When fully ripe the flesh of the fruit is yellow just like the skin.  When bletted they taste similar to tart medlars with a higher moisture content and seem very resistant to rotting (probably due to the high acid content).

description:
This is an apple tree or malus domestica and it’s found in our yard. I know this might come as a surprise, but how I know it’s an apple tree is from the fruit the tree bares, which are red apples. The tree itself is probably 18 feet tall with bark that looks gray in color with a shiny smooth-like texture. The leaves are dark green and oval with serrated edges. 

Besides it being very late September, the weather while I was observing these red beaut fruits was 67°F with a high of 70°F and a low of 51°F. It was mostly cloudy with wind around 9 mph and a humidity of 56%. 

This apple tree is very well known to the locals. White-tailed deer or odocoileus virginianus love to munch on the fruit whether they’re ripe or not. The photos seen of the deer munching were taken back in July and early August, but too cool not to share. You can also see goldenrod or solidago sp. beside the base of the tree because pollinators skip from one flower to the next to help bring the fruit.
